title: Arrays
overview: Topic 10.2 covers arrays: a list (1D array) or a table (2D array) of values of one data type, stored under one identifier and reached by an index. You need the vocabulary (element, index, lower bound, upper bound), the Cambridge declarations such as DECLARE Marks : ARRAY[1:10] OF INTEGER and DECLARE Sales : ARRAY[1:3, 1:4] OF INTEGER, and the loop patterns that process them: filling, totalling, finding the largest value, and nested loops over rows and columns. The syllabus also places two standard algorithms here: a linear search that stops when the item is found, and a bubble sort, including the efficient version that shortens each pass and stops as soon as a pass makes no swaps. Paper 2 expects these to be written from memory and dry-run with a trace table.
syllabusPoints: Use the technical terms associated with arrays, including index, upper bound and lower bound.
Select a suitable data structure (1D or 2D array) to use for a given task.
Write pseudocode to process array data, including sorting using a bubble sort and searching using a linear search.

definitions.definition: An ordered, fixed-size collection of elements that all have the same data type, stored under one identifier and accessed by index.
One item stored in an array, such as Marks[4] or Sales[2, 3].
The position number used to select an element; a 1D array uses one index and a 2D array uses a row index and a column index.
The smallest valid index of an array dimension, fixed in the declaration (often 1, sometimes 0).
The largest valid index of an array dimension; the number of elements in that dimension is upper bound - lower bound + 1.
An array with one dimension, used like a numbered list, for example ARRAY[1:10] OF INTEGER.
An array with two dimensions, used like a table of rows and columns; the row index is written first, for example Grid[Row, Column].
A search that compares the target with each element in turn from the first, stopping when it is found or when every element has been checked.
A sort that repeatedly passes through an array comparing adjacent elements and swapping any pair that is in the wrong order, until a pass makes no swaps.
One run of a bubble sort's inner loop along the unsorted part of the array; after each pass the largest remaining value has reached its final position.

sections.title: Array terms: element, index, lower bound and upper bound
content: An array lets a program keep many values of the same type under one name instead of inventing a separate variable for each. Thirty test marks stored as Mark1, Mark2 … Mark30 would need thirty INPUT statements; stored as Marks[1] to Marks[30] they can be handled by one loop whose counter supplies the position.

The position is the index. The declaration fixes the lowest index (the lower bound) and the highest index (the upper bound) for each dimension, and the array keeps that size while the program runs, so it is a static structure. Cambridge pseudocode lets you choose the bounds: many exam questions start at 1, which matches how people number a list, while Python, Java and VB.NET start their arrays at 0. Always read the bounds from the declaration rather than assuming.

The number of elements in a dimension is upper bound - lower bound + 1, so ARRAY[1:10] has 10 elements and ARRAY[0:25] has 26. An index outside the bounds refers to an element that does not exist; running such a statement causes a run-time error (an 'index out of range' or array bound error). A loop that stops one short of the upper bound does not crash but silently misses the last element, which is a logic error.
bullets: Index: the position of an element. Lower bound: smallest index. Upper bound: largest index.
Number of elements = upper bound - lower bound + 1.
Every element has the same data type; the size is fixed at declaration.
Index beyond a bound = run-time error; loop bound one too small = logic error (element skipped).

examples.label: Reading bounds from declarations
examples.content:
Declaration                              | Lower | Upper | Elements
DECLARE Letters : ARRAY[0:25] OF CHAR    | 0     | 25    | 26
DECLARE Marks : ARRAY[1:30] OF INTEGER   | 1     | 30    | 30
DECLARE Temps : ARRAY[1:7] OF REAL       | 1     | 7     | 7
DECLARE Sales : ARRAY[1:3, 1:4] OF INTEGER | rows 1-3, columns 1-4 | 3 x 4 = 12

Marks[31] ← 50 would fail at run time: 31 is above the upper bound 30.

sections.title: Declaring and using a 1D array
content: A 1D array is declared with DECLARE, the identifier, the bounds in square brackets separated by a colon, and the element type after OF. An element is then written as the identifier followed by an index in square brackets, and that element can be used anywhere an ordinary variable of the element type could be: on the left of an assignment, in an INPUT statement, in a condition or in an OUTPUT.

The index does not have to be a literal. Any INTEGER expression works, which is what makes arrays powerful: inside FOR Index ← 1 TO 7 the element Temps[Index] means a different element on each iteration. Before an array's values are used they must be given values, typically by an initialisation loop that sets every element to a starting value such as 0, or by a loop of INPUT statements. Cambridge pseudocode also allows one array to be copied into another of the same size and type in a single assignment.
bullets: DECLARE Temps : ARRAY[1:7] OF REAL gives Temps[1] to Temps[7].
Temps[3] ← 18.5 saves a value; OUTPUT Temps[3] reads it.
The index can be a variable or expression, such as Temps[Day] or Values[J + 1].
Initialise every element (with a loop) before relying on its value.

examples.label: Declaring, initialising and filling a 1D array
examples.content:
DECLARE Temps : ARRAY[1:7] OF REAL
DECLARE Day : INTEGER

// initialise every element
FOR Day ← 1 TO 7
   Temps[Day] ← 0.0
NEXT Day

// fill from input, one reading per day
FOR Day ← 1 TO 7
   OUTPUT "Temperature for day ", Day
   INPUT Temps[Day]
NEXT Day

OUTPUT "Wednesday: ", Temps[3]

sections.title: Processing a 1D array: totals, averages and the largest value
content: Most array processing is one FOR loop from the lower bound to the upper bound with the loop counter used as the index. A total needs a variable set to 0 before the loop and increased by each element inside it; an average is the total divided by the number of elements after the loop, and should be REAL.

To find the largest value, start by assuming the first element is the largest, then compare each later element with the current largest and replace it when a bigger one appears. Starting from the first element, rather than from 0, means the method also works when every value is negative. Storing the index of the largest value as well as the value lets the program report where it is.
bullets: Total: set to 0 before the loop, add each element inside the loop.
Average: Total / number of elements, calculated after the loop and stored as REAL.
Maximum: start with the first element, replace when a larger element is found; also track its index.
Loop bounds must match the declaration exactly: FOR Index ← 1 TO 6 for ARRAY[1:6].

examples.label: Total, average and highest mark
examples.content:
DECLARE Marks : ARRAY[1:6] OF INTEGER
DECLARE Index, Total, Highest, HighPos : INTEGER
DECLARE Average : REAL

// Marks holds 54, 71, 38, 90, 66, 47
Total ← 0
Highest ← Marks[1]
HighPos ← 1
FOR Index ← 1 TO 6
   Total ← Total + Marks[Index]
   IF Marks[Index] > Highest
      THEN
         Highest ← Marks[Index]
         HighPos ← Index
   ENDIF
NEXT Index
Average ← Total / 6
OUTPUT "Total ", Total, ", average ", Average
OUTPUT "Highest ", Highest, " at position ", HighPos

examples.label: Trace table: Marks = 54, 71, 38, 90, 66, 47
examples.content:
Index | Marks[Index] | Total | Highest | HighPos
      |              | 0     | 54      | 1
1     | 54           | 54    |         |
2     | 71           | 125   | 71      | 2
3     | 38           | 163   |         |
4     | 90           | 253   | 90      | 4
5     | 66           | 319   |         |
6     | 47           | 366   |         |

Average = 366 / 6 = 61.0
Output: Total 366, average 61.0
        Highest 90 at position 4
(An equivalent Python run gives the same total, average and position.)

sections.title: Linear search
content: A linear search looks for a target value by checking the elements one after another, starting at the lower bound. It needs no preparation: the data does not have to be sorted, which is why it is the standard search for an unordered array. Each check either finds the target, in which case the search can stop, or moves on to the next index. If the index passes the upper bound without a match, the target is not in the array.

A good linear search stops as soon as the item is found, so it uses a conditional loop (WHILE or REPEAT) controlled by a BOOLEAN flag such as Found and by the index reaching the end. A FOR loop over the whole array also gives the right answer but always makes every comparison, even when the target is in the first position. In the worst case (the item is last, or absent) a linear search on n elements makes n comparisons; on average it makes about half that when the item is present.
bullets: Works on unsorted data; compares elements in index order from the lower bound.
Two stopping conditions: target found, or no elements left to check.
Use a BOOLEAN Found flag and a WHILE/REPEAT loop so the search stops early.
After the loop, test Found to decide between reporting the position and reporting 'not found'.
Worst case n comparisons for n elements.

examples.label: Linear search that stops when the name is found
examples.content:
DECLARE Names : ARRAY[1:6] OF STRING
DECLARE SearchName : STRING
DECLARE Index : INTEGER
DECLARE Found : BOOLEAN

// Names holds "Ravi", "Mei", "Tomas", "Leila", "Owen", "Grace"
INPUT SearchName
Found ← FALSE
Index ← 1
WHILE Found = FALSE AND Index <= 6
   IF Names[Index] = SearchName
      THEN
         Found ← TRUE
      ELSE
         Index ← Index + 1
   ENDIF
ENDWHILE

IF Found = FALSE
   THEN
      OUTPUT SearchName, " is not in the list"
   ELSE
      OUTPUT SearchName, " is at position ", Index
ENDIF

examples.label: Trace tables: target found and target not found
examples.content:
Search 1: SearchName = "Leila"
Index | Names[Index] | Match? | Found
1     | "Ravi"       | no     | FALSE
2     | "Mei"        | no     | FALSE
3     | "Tomas"      | no     | FALSE
4     | "Leila"      | yes    | TRUE
Loop ends because Found = TRUE (4 comparisons).
Output: Leila is at position 4

Search 2: SearchName = "Sam"
Index | Names[Index] | Match? | Found
1     | "Ravi"       | no     | FALSE
2     | "Mei"        | no     | FALSE
3     | "Tomas"      | no     | FALSE
4     | "Leila"      | no     | FALSE
5     | "Owen"       | no     | FALSE
6     | "Grace"      | no     | FALSE
7     | (not read)   |        | FALSE
Loop ends because Index <= 6 is FALSE (6 comparisons). Names[7] is never accessed.
Output: Sam is not in the list

(An equivalent Python search returns position 4 after 4 comparisons and not found after 6.)

sections.title: Bubble sort
content: A bubble sort puts an array into order by comparing neighbouring elements. Starting at the lower bound, it compares elements 1 and 2 and swaps them if the first is larger, then compares 2 and 3, and so on to the end. That complete run is one pass. During a pass the largest value keeps being swapped forward, so at the end of the first pass it sits in the last element, which is now final. The next pass does the same for the rest of the array, placing the second largest value, and so on.

Swapping two elements needs a temporary variable: copy the first element to Temp, copy the second into the first, then copy Temp into the second. Without Temp, the first value would be overwritten and lost.

For an array of n elements, n - 1 passes are always enough. Because the end of the array fills up with finished values, each pass can stop one position earlier than the last; a variable (here Boundary) holds the last index to compare and is reduced by 1 after every pass. The algorithm uses nested loops: the outer loop counts passes and the inner loop moves along the array comparing pairs. To sort into descending order, change the comparison from > to <.
bullets: Compare adjacent pairs; swap if Values[J] > Values[J + 1] (ascending).
A swap uses Temp: Temp ← a, a ← b, b ← Temp.
After pass k the largest k values are in their final positions at the end of the array.
At most n - 1 passes; the inner loop's end can be reduced by 1 after each pass.
Descending order: use < in the comparison.

examples.label: Bubble sort with a fixed number of passes
examples.content:
DECLARE Values : ARRAY[1:5] OF INTEGER
DECLARE Pass, J, Boundary, Temp : INTEGER

// Values holds 7, 3, 9, 1, 5
Boundary ← 4                       // last J to compare: upper bound - 1
FOR Pass ← 1 TO 4                  // n - 1 passes
   FOR J ← 1 TO Boundary
      IF Values[J] > Values[J + 1]
         THEN
            Temp ← Values[J]
            Values[J] ← Values[J + 1]
            Values[J + 1] ← Temp
      ENDIF
   NEXT J
   Boundary ← Boundary - 1         // last element of this pass is now final
NEXT Pass

examples.label: Array state during and after each pass: 7, 3, 9, 1, 5
examples.content:
Pass 1 (J = 1 to 4)
  J=1: 7 > 3 swap  -> 3 7 9 1 5
  J=2: 7 > 9 no    -> 3 7 9 1 5
  J=3: 9 > 1 swap  -> 3 7 1 9 5
  J=4: 9 > 5 swap  -> 3 7 1 5 9     9 is now final
Pass 2 (J = 1 to 3)
  J=1: 3 > 7 no    -> 3 7 1 5 9
  J=2: 7 > 1 swap  -> 3 1 7 5 9
  J=3: 7 > 5 swap  -> 3 1 5 7 9     7 is now final
Pass 3 (J = 1 to 2)
  J=1: 3 > 1 swap  -> 1 3 5 7 9
  J=2: 3 > 5 no    -> 1 3 5 7 9
Pass 4 (J = 1 to 1)
  J=1: 1 > 3 no    -> 1 3 5 7 9

After pass: 1: 3 7 1 5 9 | 2: 3 1 5 7 9 | 3: 1 3 5 7 9 | 4: 1 3 5 7 9
Comparisons: 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10. Pass 4 changes nothing: the array was already sorted after pass 3.
(An equivalent Python run produces the same four states and 10 comparisons.)

sections.title: Efficient bubble sort: a swap flag and shorter passes
content: The fixed-pass version keeps going even after the data is in order. The improvement rests on one observation: if a whole pass makes no swaps, every adjacent pair is already in order, so the array is sorted and the algorithm can stop. A BOOLEAN flag records this. It is set to TRUE (no swaps yet) at the start of each pass and set to FALSE whenever a swap happens; the outer loop becomes a REPEAT … UNTIL that ends when a pass finishes with the flag still TRUE.

Keeping the reducing boundary as well gives the efficient bubble sort that mark schemes look for: a conditional outer loop, the flag reset at the start of each pass, the flag changed inside the swap, and the inner loop's end reduced after each pass. On nearly sorted data it can finish after one or two passes; on already sorted data it needs just one pass of n - 1 comparisons. Its worst case (data in reverse order) is still about n²/2 comparisons, which is why bubble sort is only used for small arrays.

The same idea works on a 2D array or an array of records. When sorting rows of a table by one column, compare that column and swap the entire row (every column), or with an array of records swap whole records, so that each item's data stays together.
bullets: NoSwaps ← TRUE at the start of each pass; NoSwaps ← FALSE inside the swap.
Outer loop: REPEAT … UNTIL NoSwaps = TRUE (stops early once sorted).
Boundary ← Boundary - 1 after each pass so finished values are not compared again.
Best case (already sorted): one pass. Worst case (reverse order): n - 1 passes.
When sorting a table by one column, swap the whole row, not just the compared value.

examples.label: Efficient bubble sort
examples.content:
DECLARE Values : ARRAY[1:6] OF INTEGER
DECLARE J, Boundary, Temp : INTEGER
DECLARE NoSwaps : BOOLEAN

Boundary ← 5                       // upper bound - 1
REPEAT
   NoSwaps ← TRUE
   FOR J ← 1 TO Boundary
      IF Values[J] > Values[J + 1]
         THEN
            Temp ← Values[J]
            Values[J] ← Values[J + 1]
            Values[J + 1] ← Temp
            NoSwaps ← FALSE
      ENDIF
   NEXT J
   Boundary ← Boundary - 1
UNTIL NoSwaps = TRUE

examples.label: Trace: nearly sorted data 3, 1, 4, 6, 5, 8
examples.content:
Pass 1 (Boundary = 5), NoSwaps starts TRUE
  J=1: 3 > 1 swap -> 1 3 4 6 5 8   NoSwaps = FALSE
  J=2: 3 > 4 no
  J=3: 4 > 6 no
  J=4: 6 > 5 swap -> 1 3 4 5 6 8   NoSwaps = FALSE
  J=5: 6 > 8 no
  end of pass: 1 3 4 5 6 8, Boundary becomes 4, NoSwaps = FALSE so repeat
Pass 2 (Boundary = 4), NoSwaps starts TRUE
  J=1..4: 1>3, 3>4, 4>5, 5>6 all no
  end of pass: 1 3 4 5 6 8, NoSwaps = TRUE so UNTIL ends the sort

Efficient version: 2 passes, 5 + 4 = 9 comparisons.
Fixed-pass version on the same data: 5 passes, 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15 comparisons.
For 7, 3, 9, 1, 5 the flag version still needs 4 passes (10 comparisons), because pass 3 made a swap.
(Checked with an equivalent Python run.)

examples.label: Python equivalent used to check the traces

sections.title: Declaring and using a 2D array
content: A 2D array stores a table. Its declaration gives two pairs of bounds separated by a comma: the first pair is for the rows and the second for the columns, following the usual convention of naming the row first when you describe a cell of a table. DECLARE Sales : ARRAY[1:3, 1:4] OF INTEGER creates 3 rows and 4 columns, 12 elements in all, and every element must be an INTEGER.

An element is reached with two indexes in the same order: Sales[2, 3] is row 2, column 3. Mixing up the order is one of the most frequent errors; with a non-square table it may even produce an out-of-range index. As with 1D arrays the bounds are chosen by the programmer: rows and columns starting at 1 often match the problem (shop 1 to 3, quarter 1 to 4, a game board of rows 1 to 6).
bullets: DECLARE Name : ARRAY[RowLower:RowUpper, ColLower:ColUpper] OF Type.
Element count = rows x columns, e.g. 3 x 4 = 12.
Access as Name[Row, Column], row index first.
All elements share one data type.

examples.label: A 3 by 4 table of quarterly sales
examples.content:
DECLARE Sales : ARRAY[1:3, 1:4] OF INTEGER   // 3 shops (rows), 4 quarters (columns)

Sales[1, 1] ← 12      // shop 1, quarter 1
Sales[2, 3] ← 14      // shop 2, quarter 3
OUTPUT Sales[2, 3]     // 14

sections.title: Processing a 2D array with nested loops
content: Visiting every element of a table needs a loop inside a loop. The outer loop selects a row; for each row the inner loop runs through all the columns before the outer loop moves on, so the elements are visited row by row. The same pattern initialises a table, outputs it one row per line, or totals it.

Where a total is set matters. A total for each row is reset to 0 inside the outer loop but before the inner loop, and output after the inner loop finishes. A grand total is set to 0 once, before both loops. A column total swaps the roles: the outer loop runs over columns and the inner loop over rows.
bullets: Outer loop = rows, inner loop = columns, element = Table[Row, Column].
Row total: reset inside the outer loop, before the inner loop; output after the inner loop.
Grand total: reset once before both loops.
Column totals: make the column the outer loop.

examples.label: Row totals and grand total
examples.content:
DECLARE Sales : ARRAY[1:3, 1:4] OF INTEGER
DECLARE Shop, Quarter, ShopTotal, GrandTotal : INTEGER

// Sales holds  row 1: 12 15  9 20
//              row 2:  8 11 14  6
//              row 3: 17  5 10 13
GrandTotal ← 0
FOR Shop ← 1 TO 3
   ShopTotal ← 0
   FOR Quarter ← 1 TO 4
      ShopTotal ← ShopTotal + Sales[Shop, Quarter]
   NEXT Quarter
   OUTPUT "Shop ", Shop, ": ", ShopTotal
   GrandTotal ← GrandTotal + ShopTotal
NEXT Shop
OUTPUT "All shops: ", GrandTotal

examples.label: Trace of the row totals
examples.content:
Shop | Quarter values added   | ShopTotal | GrandTotal | OUTPUT
     |                        |           | 0          |
1    | 12, 15, 9, 20          | 56        | 56         | Shop 1: 56
2    | 8, 11, 14, 6           | 39        | 95         | Shop 2: 39
3    | 17, 5, 10, 13          | 45        | 140        | Shop 3: 45
                                                      | All shops: 140

Inside row 1 the running ShopTotal is 12, 27, 36, 56.
Column (quarter) totals, with Quarter as the outer loop: 37, 31, 33, 39, which also sum to 140.
(An equivalent Python run with nested lists gives the same row, column and grand totals.)

sections.title: Selecting a 1D or 2D array for a task
content: Choose a 1D array when the data is a single list of values of one type identified by one number: the daily rainfall for a month, the names in a register, a list of scores to sort. Choose a 2D array when each value is identified by two things at once and all the values have the same type: sales by shop and quarter, marks by student and test, the cells of a game board or a seating plan.

Parallel 1D arrays (for example Names[1:30] and Marks[1:30] matched by index) can hold related data of different types, but they must be kept in step by hand, which is fragile when sorting. A 2D array cannot help here because all its elements must share one type; if a table would mix types, such as a name column and a mark column, use an array of records instead (see 10.1).
bullets: One list, one index: 1D array.
Values located by two coordinates (row and column), all the same type: 2D array.
Related values of different types per item: array of records, or parallel 1D arrays kept in step.
Justify the choice from the data: how many indexes identify a value, and are the types the same?

examples.label: Choosing the structure
examples.content:
Task                                               | Structure                              | Reason
Rainfall for each day of June                      | ARRAY[1:30] OF REAL                    | one list, one index (day)
Marks of 25 students in 6 tests                    | ARRAY[1:25, 1:6] OF INTEGER            | two indexes (student, test), all INTEGER
Noughts and crosses board                          | ARRAY[1:3, 1:3] OF CHAR                | cell found by row and column
Names to be sorted into order                      | ARRAY[1:40] OF STRING                  | one list
Name, form and date of birth for each student      | ARRAY[1:40] OF StudentRecord           | different types per student, so not a 2D array

sections.title: Checking loops against bounds
content: Every loop over an array should be checked against the declaration. For ARRAY[1:6], FOR Index ← 0 TO 6 reads the non-existent element 0 and FOR Index ← 1 TO 7 reads element 7: both stop the program with a run-time error when that line executes. FOR Index ← 1 TO 5 runs without error but never processes element 6, which gives a wrong answer and is a logic error.

Bubble sort needs particular care, because the comparison uses Values[J + 1]. The inner loop must stop at the upper bound minus 1 (then minus the number of passes completed), otherwise J + 1 goes past the upper bound. In a linear search with a WHILE loop, test the index before using it, so that the loop ends when the index passes the upper bound rather than trying to read a missing element.
bullets: Loop from exactly the lower bound to exactly the upper bound for a full traversal.
In comparisons using J + 1, the loop must end one before the upper bound.
Out-of-range index: run-time error. Missing an element: logic error.

examples.label: Spot the error: bubble sort inner loop
examples.content:
DECLARE Values : ARRAY[1:5] OF INTEGER
FOR J ← 1 TO 5
   IF Values[J] > Values[J + 1] ...

When J = 5 the condition reads Values[6], which is beyond the upper bound 5,
so the program fails at run time. Correct first pass: FOR J ← 1 TO 4.

comparisonTable.title: Linear search and bubble sort compared
rows: Find the position of a target value, or report it is absent
Put the elements into ascending (or descending) order
One conditional loop (WHILE or REPEAT) with a Found flag
REPEAT … UNTIL NoSwaps = TRUE around a FOR loop over adjacent pairs
Target found, or index passes the upper bound

diagram.title: One pass of an efficient bubble sort
nodes: Set NoSwaps to TRUE; J starts at the lower bound
If out of order: swap via Temp and set NoSwaps to FALSE
Move J on by 1 until J reaches Boundary
Reduce Boundary by 1 (last compared position is now final)
If NoSwaps is still TRUE the array is sorted; otherwise start another pass

analysisChains.title: Why a FOR loop is a weaker linear search
steps: A search is written as FOR Index ← 1 TO 1000 with IF Items[Index] = Target THEN Found ← TRUE
The FOR loop still makes all 1000 comparisons, because it cannot stop early
Rewriting with WHILE Found = FALSE AND Index <= 1000 ends the loop after 3 comparisons
analysisChains.evaluation: Both versions give the correct result, but the conditional loop does less work on average, which is why mark schemes reward a loop that terminates when the item is found.

analysisChains.title: Why the efficient bubble sort is worth the extra variable
steps: The data 3, 1, 4, 6, 5, 8 is almost in order
Pass 1 swaps (3,1) and (6,5) and the array becomes 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8
Pass 2 makes no swaps, so NoSwaps stays TRUE and the REPEAT loop ends
The fixed version would carry on for three more passes that change nothing
analysisChains.evaluation: The flag costs one BOOLEAN and two assignments but cuts the work from 15 to 9 comparisons here; the saving grows with larger, nearly sorted arrays, though reverse-ordered data gains nothing.

analysisChains.title: Choosing the structure for exam results
steps: A school stores, for 200 candidates, a candidate number and a mark
Both are whole numbers, so a 2D array ARRAY[1:200, 1:2] OF INTEGER is possible, with column 1 the number and column 2 the mark
To sort by mark, the bubble sort compares column 2 but must swap both columns of the two rows
If candidate names (STRING) were added, a 2D array could no longer hold the data, so an array of records would be needed
analysisChains.evaluation: A 2D array suits a table whose values all share one type; once the columns need different types, the data should move to an array of records, which also makes whole-row swaps a single assignment.

examTips: Read the bounds from the declaration before writing any loop: a FOR loop over ARRAY[1:50] runs 1 TO 50, while ARRAY[0:49] runs 0 TO 49.
For a linear search, use a conditional loop with a Found flag so the search stops when the item is found, and after the loop output either the position or a 'not found' message.

For an efficient bubble sort the marks usually come from: an outer conditional loop, an inner loop over adjacent pairs, a correct comparison, a swap through Temp, resetting the flag each pass, setting it on a swap, and reducing the inner loop's end.
When writing a 2D array element, put the row index first, and in nested loops make the outer loop the one whose total is reset or output after each group.
When asked to trace a bubble sort, show the full array after every pass (or after every swap if asked); examiners check intermediate states, not just the final order.
commonMistakes: Assuming every array starts at index 0 (or at 1) instead of using the bounds in the declaration.
Letting the bubble sort's inner loop run to the upper bound, so Values[J + 1] is out of range.
Swapping without a temporary variable (Values[J] ← Values[J + 1] then Values[J + 1] ← Values[J]), which copies one value into both elements.
Setting NoSwaps once before the outer loop instead of resetting it at the start of every pass, so the sort never stops or stops too early.
Outputting 'not found' inside the search loop for every non-matching element instead of once after the loop.
Writing Table[Column, Row], or resetting a row total outside the outer loop so it keeps accumulating across rows.

quickRecall.question: Define lower bound and upper bound.
quickRecall.answer: The smallest and the largest valid index of an array dimension, as given in its declaration.

quickRecall.question: How many elements does DECLARE Codes : ARRAY[0:25] OF CHAR create?
Declare a 2D array of integers with 3 rows and 4 columns, indexed from 1.
What are the two conditions that end a linear search?
quickRecall.answer: The target has been found, or every element has been checked (the index has passed the upper bound).

quickRecall.question: What is true about the array after the first pass of an ascending bubble sort?
quickRecall.answer: The largest value is in the last position, which will not change again.

quickRecall.question: Why is a temporary variable needed in a swap?
quickRecall.answer: Assigning the second element to the first overwrites the first value; Temp keeps a copy so it can be put into the second element.

quickRecall.question: How does the efficient bubble sort know it can stop?
quickRecall.answer: A flag set to TRUE at the start of each pass is still TRUE at the end, meaning no swaps happened, so every adjacent pair is in order.

quickRecall.question: When is a 2D array more suitable than a 1D array?
quickRecall.answer: When each value is identified by two indexes, such as row and column, and all the values have the same data type.
